result.summary: Pentheus scorns the prophet Tiresias and the new god Bacchus (Liber), and orders Bacchus's follower Acoetes seized. Acoetes tells how sailors who kidnapped the disguised god were turned into dolphins. Pentheus spies on the rites at Cithaeron and is torn apart by his mother Agave and her sisters.

scenes.title: Pentheus mocks Tiresias
scenes.summary: Tiresias warns Pentheus that he will be torn apart if he rejects Bacchus. Pentheus drives him away.
scenes.stakes: Pentheus risks the god's wrath and a violent death by refusing him honor.

scenes.title: Pentheus rages against Bacchus
scenes.summary: Crowds join the Bacchic rites. Pentheus harangues the Thebans, ignores Cadmus and Athamas, and has Acoetes brought in chains.
scenes.stakes: Thebes's people may abandon their old ways; Pentheus risks ruin by defying the god.

scenes.title: Acoetes tells of the ship
scenes.summary: Acoetes tells how the crew seized a drunken boy who was Bacchus and tried to deceive him. The god wrecked their ship with ivy and turned them into dolphins.
scenes.stakes: The sailors risk the god's vengeance. Acoetes risks being thrown overboard.

scenes.title: Acoetes imprisoned and freed
scenes.summary: Pentheus orders Acoetes tortured. Acoetes is jailed, but the doors and chains open by themselves.

scenes.title: Death of Pentheus on Cithaeron
scenes.summary: Pentheus goes to Cithaeron to watch the rites. His mother Agave, Autonoe and Ino tear him apart, mistaking him for a boar. Thebes then honors Bacchus.
scenes.stakes: Pentheus's life is lost to the frenzied women.

alias_notes.explanation: Liber is the Latin name of Bacchus, the god of wine.

notable_quotes.reason: Memorable simile of a torrent growing fiercer when obstructed, like Pentheus.
Pentheus's pitiful cry to his mother as she dismembers him.

analysis.text: Rejecting a god brings destruction. Pentheus's pride and blindness contrast with the blind prophet's insight.
The story reflects Greek anxiety about the arrival of Dionysiac worship, with its ecstatic rites, and about resistance to it.

legacy.text: The story of Pentheus and Dionysus was dramatized by Euripides in The Bacchae, which Ovid draws on.
The tale of the sailors turned into dolphins appears in the Homeric Hymn to Dionysus, and Ovid's version retells it.

fun_facts.text: Ovid gives the god's hostile captors dolphin forms, linking the myth to the dolphin's association with Dionysus.

language_notes.text: Tiresias's fame came from his earlier prophecy about Narcissus, told just before this scene. Achaia here means Greece generally.
Liber is a Latin name for Bacchus, god of wine and ecstatic rites. Semele was his mortal mother.
"Vouchsafe" means to grant graciously. Here Tiresias warns Pentheus to grant Bacchus a temple.
Descendants of the Dragon: the Thebans sprang from dragon's teeth sown by Cadmus, producing armed men. Pentheus invokes this origin.
A new Tyre: Cadmus came from Tyre in Phoenicia and founded Thebes, bringing his household gods with him.
The thyrsus was a staff tipped with a pine cone and wreathed in ivy or vine leaves, carried by Bacchic worshippers.
Acrisius, king of Argos, had resisted Bacchus's worship. Pentheus cites him as a model of resistance.
The Etrurian prisoner is Acoetes, who is Bacchus in disguise, as the opening summary says.
Mæonia is an old name for Lydia in Asia Minor, so Acœtes is introducing himself as a Lydian of humble birth.
The Olenian she-goat is Capella, a star associated with storms. Taygete (a Pleiad), the Hyades and the Bear are other stars sailors steered by.
Dia is an old name for the island later called Naxos. This explains why Bacchus later tells Acœtes to make for Dia.
Epopeus is the crew's rhythm-keeper, who calls the stroke so the oars move in time.
Liber is another name for Bacchus, the Roman god of wine. The text uses both names for the same god.
Ivy and the vine are sacred to Bacchus. Their sudden growth over the ship signals the god's power.
Stygian refers to the Styx, river of the underworld; 'Stygian night' means the darkness of death.
Etrurian means from Etruria, in Italy. Acœtes had told Pentheus he was a Lydian-born sailor who later lived in Etruria.
'The son of Echion' is Pentheus, identified by his father, one of the Sown Men of Thebes.
A thyrsus is a staff topped with a pine cone and wound with ivy, carried by followers of Bacchus.
Actæon was Pentheus's cousin, torn apart by his own hounds after seeing Diana bathing. Pentheus hopes this memory will make his aunt spare him.
Ismenian means Theban, from the river Ismenus near Thebes.

context_notes.text: Tiresias was the blind Theban prophet. Pentheus is Bacchus's cousin, since both are grandsons of Cadmus.
Cadmus, Pentheus's grandfather, founded Thebes. Athamas was a relative, Cadmus's son-in-law.
Etruria was a region of central Italy. Lycabas is an exile for murder, which marks him as violent and lawless.
Bacchus, god of wine, ecstasy and theatre, had been disguised as a drunken boy. Here he reveals himself.
The sailors turn into dolphins. This transformation is the punishment for their impiety and treachery toward the god.
Cithæron is the mountain near Thebes where Bacchic rites were held. It is also linked with other Theban myths.
Agave, Pentheus's mother, is a Theban princess. Bacchus's madness makes her and her sisters see her son as a boar.

literary_notes.text: Tiresias turns the insult about blindness around: the blind seer sees more truly than Pentheus, who can see but not understand.
The prophecy of being scattered and torn apart anticipates Pentheus's death at the hands of his own mother and aunts.
Pentheus piles up contemptuous questions, showing his scorn for Bacchic worship as unmanly and his habit of arguing by insult.
The torrent obstructed by beams and stones compares Pentheus's fury to water, showing that opposition only makes him more violent.
The narrator's closing remark states the theme plainly: greed for plunder blinds the crew to the obvious divinity of the boy.
The sailors swear by all the gods to deceive a god, making their false oaths especially impious.
Bacchus is described as 'like one weeping'. This feigned sorrow makes him seem a vulnerable boy while he exposes the crew's deceit.
The curved tail is compared to the horns of the half-moon, giving a vivid image of the half-finished transformation.
The sharp opposition between twenty men and one survivor makes the scale of the punishment clear.
Pentheus's anger is compared to a war-horse excited by the trumpet, which shows how the noise inflames him.
The reader knows the 'boar' is Pentheus, and that his profane watching has caused the delusion.
His appeal to Actæon fails because Autonoë cannot understand it, so the warning of a similar fate has no effect.
Pentheus's body is compared to autumn leaves stripped from a tree, which makes the dismemberment seem quick and easy.
